rv.q: The production, though sadly undermined by its flaws, is bleakly spectacular.
Striking, austere visuals and star casting can’t bring heart to this cold and incoherent take on Shakespeare’s story of magic, legacy and forgiveness.
All-in-all it’s a stylish mix of good ideas and bad ideas.
This production certainly has some striking moments but far too many underwhelming ones, and if you come out remembering Ariel rather than Prospero, something is amiss.
For all its stark visual boldness, this is a curiously old-fashioned take.
It is hard to imagine a staging that mingles so much bombast with so much fog.
Those unfamiliar with the play will be bamboozled from start to finish, such is the lack of clarity and conviction with which the narrative treated.
This production may well be loved by some but hated by others.
There’s little substance in this production, but plenty of style.
So it’s not overly surprising that the star of “Alien” and “Avatar” might choose to come to the West End in “The Tempest,” Shakespeare’s otherworldly play.
And despite this production’s flaws, the audience reacts kindly to Prospero’s adieu.
The entire production is stripped of poetry or wonder but doesn’t offer any alternative revelation in its place.
This bad idea has been adopted by Jamie Lloyd in his cheerless version starring Sigourney Weaver.
But it's not enough to save this Tempest. I suppose I must applaud Lloyd for pushing the boat out. But this production is lost at sea.
However, when it comes to delivering the lines, her performance feels flat and often unclear.

cn.t: Jamie Lloyd's stark production and Sigourney Weaver's West End debut as Prospero disappoint critics, who find the staging misconceived and the star performance flat and lacking charisma despite an impressive opening.
